title: Keeping a three-week branch alive without a conflict festival
summary: Sometimes a long branch is unavoidable. Compare the two ways to keep it current — merging main in repeatedly, or rebasing onto main — and see exactly what each does to the diff a reviewer reads.
concepts: merge main in vs rebase onto main
mental_model: Both strategies keep you current; they differ in what they leave behind. Merging preserves shas and litters the branch with merge commits. Rebasing rewrites shas and keeps the branch a clean series — but force-pushes every time.

commit.message: Raise the timeout after the incident

steps.title: Turn on rerere before you start
steps.why: A long branch hits the same conflict on every sync. rerere records your first resolution and replays it, which turns the second, third and fourth sync from painful into automatic.

steps.title: Strategy one: merge main into the branch
steps.why: This keeps every sha stable, so a reviewer's place in the diff survives and nobody needs to force-push. The cost is a merge commit in the branch, and the branch's own history becomes harder to read.
steps.expect: A conflict on the TIMEOUT line — main raised it while you were restructuring.

steps.title: Resolve it, keeping both intentions
steps.why: Take main's new timeout and your class structure. rerere records this resolution against the conflict's fingerprint, which is what makes the next step interesting.

verify.label: the branch now carries a merge commit

steps.title: Strategy two: rebase the branch onto main
steps.why: Same starting point, different verb. Your two commits are replayed on top of main's new commit, so the branch stays a clean linear series with no merge commit at all.
steps.expect: The same conflict — but rerere resolves it for you automatically this time.

verify.label: rerere replayed the resolution during the rebase
verify.hint: enable rerere before the first conflict, not after

steps.title: Finish the rebase
steps.why: rerere resolved the file but deliberately left it unstaged, so you still get to look. Stage and continue — and note you did not have to think about the conflict a second time.

verify.label: the rebased branch is a clean two-commit series

steps.title: Compare what a reviewer reads
steps.why: Identical code, different reading experience. The merged branch shows three commits including a merge; the rebased one shows two commits that apply cleanly to current main. For review, the second is unambiguously better.
steps.expect: No file differences at all — only the history differs.

steps.title: Choose by whether the branch is shared
steps.why: Rebase while the branch is yours alone; merge once other people have pulled it. That single rule resolves nearly every argument about which is correct — they are correct in different situations.
steps.expect: Nothing further to run; the decision is social, not technical.

verify.label: the rebased branch is a clean series on top of current main
the merged branch carries a merge commit instead
rerere made the second conflict resolve itself

pitfalls: Rebasing a branch other people have pulled forces them into a painful reconciliation. Once shared, merge.
Syncing weekly means weekly conflicts of increasing size. Syncing daily means daily conflicts of trivial size. The cadence matters more than the strategy.
Without rerere, a long-lived rebase makes you resolve the same conflict on every sync. Turn it on globally and forget it.
If a branch needs three weeks, ask whether it can ship in pieces behind a flag instead. The best fix for long-branch pain is a shorter branch.
cheatsheet: sync by merging — stable shas, merge commits
sync by rebasing — clean series, new shas
